newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION - WAYS TO REVIVE INDIAN COTTON INDUSTRY - EICA VIEW.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - WAYS TO REVIVE INDIAN COTTON INDUSTRY - EICA VIEW.

text.p: The following are extracts from a speech of Suresh A.Kotak, president of The East India Cotton Association, delivered at the associatio's 74th annual general meeting on September 6, 1996 in Bombay.
COTTON'S VITAL ROLE:

Among the annual crops, cotton has a unique place in India because it is not only the principal cash crop, and in fact the only real cash crop in the dry farming regions, but it also sustains the country's foremost industry which accounts for one-fifth of the total industrial output and one-third of the total foreign exchange earnings.

Although the crop has made tremendous strides in recent years, problems facing it are galore, the most vexed one being the low per hectare productivity. Even during 1995/96, when the country harvested an all-time high crop exceeding 15.7 miillion bales, the average yield was just about 310 kg per hectare, in contrast to the world average of 560 kg during the same year. This gives an idea of the leeway we have to make to catch up with the rest of the world.
GALVANISE EXTENSION MACHINERY:

The important point, however, is that the potential to raise productivity to world standards does exist. A number of progressive farmers in the country regularly harvest crops of 25-30 quintals of seed cotton or 835-1000 kg lint per hectare from irrigated areas and about 10-12 quintals of kapas of 350-400 kg lint per hectare in the assured rainfall areas.

The main reason behind the national average being dismally low is that the improved production technology has still not permeated to the level of ordinary farmers in several tracts. In fact, even a basic and non-monetary input like pure seed is not available to the farmers on the scale needed.

It is, therefore, essential that the States should galvanise their agriculture extension machinery to reach the know-how to the farmers in the remote villages and also considerably strengthen the infrastructure for supply of the essential inputs.

In the present context of globalisation of economy, the crucial point is cost efficient production of raw materials so that farmers' income is boosted not by inflated prices but by increased productivity per unit area.
COTTON EXPORT POLICY:

The government has released a record quota of 1.49 million bales of raw cotton for export in 1995/96. However, hardly 0.8 million bales are expected to be actually shipped. This is chiefly due to the fact that inspite of the liberalisation process, export quotas are still being released in fits and starts.

The on-again, off-again policy in cotton export is not conducive for expanding our international trade in cotton since the foreign buyers lose their confidence and look to sources elsewhere to cover their requirement although price-wise and quality-wise Indian cotton is extremely competitive.

These hesistant policies of releasing of small quotas at a time and even that at the fag end of the season, when the overseas buyers have already covered their requirement, do not help us in taking full advantage of the world cotton market.

In the process, we also let slip a good opportunity to earn precious foreign exchange. It is time we shed the blinkers of the past and took bold decisions regarding cotton export in keeping with the liberalised policy environment that we visualise.
PROFILED STUDY OF CROP NEEDED:

Whenever we consider the demand-supply situation in cotton, we invariably take the total crop size into consideration and not in terms of its profile according to the staple groups. It is on the basis of such an overall view that decisions on surplus or deficit are taken.

However, a profiled study of the production would reveal that in certain staple categories, like the coarse and short staple groups, there are regular and sizable surpluses every year. Some of the coarse types are not even utilised by the textile industry.

Often, the surplus situation in the case of such cottons leads to a slump in their market prices and as a reaction to such a slump, there is a tendency to mix them with superior cottons to realise better prices while marketing.
If, however, we allow such surplus cottons to be siphoned off through free exports, not only can this malpractice be prevented but the country can also earn precious foreign exchange in the process.
What is more, it will not affect the textile industry in any way. To get this unwanted cotton immobilised within the country is nothing but a national waste of the precious resources of the country.
SUPPORT SYSTEMS NEEDED:
It has been said that in the quota-free post-W.T.O. world, India will be in a position to capture a sizable share of the world market in cotton and textiles.

This is true but it is not without a rider. Indeed, India has all the ingredients to emerge as a major player in the world textile market but if we are to do so, it is imperative that we take immediate steps to remove the several problems that plague not only the production of the crop but also its marketing and processing.
In the past, Indian cotton had a cloistered existence since there was a captive market within the country both for cotton and the textile goods made from it.

The situation has in recent years undergone a radical change and the country has been able to establish a beach-head in the world cotton and textile market. We have the capacity to considerably enlarge this beach-head but the cutting edge would have to be quality and price competitiveness.

If we are to acquire this edge, the much needed support systems will have to be provided. Permit me to dwell briefly on some of these which cover inputs, parking of cotton, credit facility, risk bearing and processing.
INPUT SUPPORT:
The basic requirement is for supply of essential inputs like good quality seed. Several agencies in the state and private sectors are now engaged in seed production in a limited way.

Still, a large area is planted with market seed of doubtful purity and low viability. What is needed is a well coordinated and much bigger efforts by all agencies by pooling their expertise and resources backed by greater financial support from the Government so that maximum area under cotton is planted with pure, good quality seed of the varieties recommended for each region.
SUPPORT FOR COTTON PARKING:
Between the 70's and now, our crop size has more than doubled, with the 1995/96 crop placed at around 15.7 million bales.

However, the infrastructure available in different centres is woefully inadequate for parking a crop of this magnitude. The result is high contamination and considerable deterioration in grade and quality and waste due to stacking of kapas in the open where it is exposed to the elements of nature. We can ill afford to allow such waste and degradation of a precious resource material.

Adequate cotton parking system should therefore be built up by strengthening the warehousing and storage facilities in all the producing and marketing centres. The land and financial resources required for the purpose need to be provided by the Government.
FINANCIAL SUPPORT:
Despite repeated pleas, cotton has still not been taken out of the selective credit control regime, although some minor relief by way of reduced margins has been provided.
Over 70 percent of the crop is being marketed by the private trade and at the present level of prices and crop size, the finance required is of the order of 120,000 million rupee.

The trade is, however, severely handicapped in mobilising the needed credit because of the rigours of control. Not only is the margin still high but there is also problem due to imposition of ceilings.
Cotton trade is even denied the facility of usance bills of 60-120 days under the Bill Market Scheme since the advances are linked to credit control.
Selective credit control is basically an anti-hoarding measure and in an environment of abundant supplies and rapid increase in production, it is apparently an anachronism in the case of cotton.

Moreover, while imposition of such control in the case of food articles which are daily household necessities may have an aura of justification, it is irrelevant in the case of an industrial raw material.

It is also pertinent to mention that no other raw material of the textile industry like fibres and yarns of viscose, polyester and acrylic is subjected to credit control. Thus, singling out cotton for such control is apparently not only unjustified but also discriminatory.

I take the opportunity to make a fervent appeal to the highest authorities of the Reserve Bank to remove this irritant which not only disrupts the smooth marketing of cotton but also adds to the marketing cost that is in the interest of neither the producer nor the consumer.
SUPPORT FOR RAW COTTON PROCESSING:

Raw cotton processing is a major sector that cries for support. While the country has made remarkable strides in the production and quality upgradation of cotton and vast changes by way of expansion and modernisation have taken place in the textile industry, improvements in the intermediate sector of raw cotton processing have been minimal.

The bulk of the machinery is of old vintage, their maintenance poor and there is very little automation. Work practices followed by the labour leave very much to be desired and the covered and uncovered storage space is grossly inadequate in many factories.
The net result is that the bales turned out by many factories have high contamination and since the packaging is not properly done, they get further contaminated during transport over long distances.
Although the need for bringing about the overdue improvements have been keenly felt, financial constraints and other inherent problems stand in the way.
Internal resource mobilisation in this sector can be only very low as the activity is seasonal and profit margins quite moderate.

It is essential that Government and Financial Institutions like NABARD give serious thought to the improvement of this sector and provide adequate financial support through soft loans, duty concessions etc.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
